# Zechariah 6: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I couldn't cover:** My tools ran out before I could read pages from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, catholic.com, any Lutheran site (lcms.org, 1517.org) or a clearly Pentecostal site. I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching for this chapter. Those areas are left out. Each tradition label below refers to the commentator named, not to an official church position.

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 1–3 (the four chariots and the bronze mountains)**
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) says that because the Hebrew reads "*the* two mountains," most readers take them to be the Mount of Olives and Mount Zion. He says bronze links the mountains with strength and judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Guzik contrasts these chariots with the horsemen of chapter 1. Those riders were scouts. These chariots seem to be hostile agents of God's judgment, emissaries of His war against the earth. He quotes Luck: red stands for war, black for famine and death, white for victory, and dappled for pestilence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Calvin says the mountains stand for the providence of God, or his hidden counsel. They are bronze because God's decree cannot be broken. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-1.html
- Matthew Henry makes a pastoral point: whatever God's providences are, we should see them all coming from between the mountains of brass. That means we should accept them, not quarrel with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-1.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the two mountains probably can't be identified. It reads the bronze as a picture of how firm the theocracy is, and the number four as completeness: the judgment shall leave no quarter unvisited. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/6-1.htm
- John Wesley takes the chariots to be angels, who are sometimes called God's chariots. He reads the red horses as bloody times, black as death and disease, white as good times, and grizzled as a mixed state of affairs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html
- Constable says chariots were instruments of judgment and that bronze often carries that meaning in Scripture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-1.html

**v. 4 (the prophet's question)**
- The Bible Says notes that the chariots' different colours caught Zechariah's attention and made him curious, so he asked the angel what they were. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/zec-6-v1-8.cfm

**v. 5 ("four spirits of heaven")**
- Guzik takes this to mean the chariots were actually four angelic beings sent from God. He quotes Calvin: they are pictured as riders because they move swiftly through the world to carry out God's commands. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Wesley says these are the angels of heaven, who have a large part in managing the affairs of the church and of nations. "Standing" pictures servants waiting for their Lord's command. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html
- A Bible Hub article notes that the Hebrew word can mean either "winds" or "spirits." https://biblehub.com/q/What_do_Zechariah_s_4_chariots_mean.htm

**v. 6 (north and south)**
- Wesley identifies the "north country" as Babylon and the "south country" as Egypt and Arabia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html
- Keil and Delitzsch read the north (the lands of the Euphrates and Tigris) and the south (Egypt) as the two main seats of world power hostile to Israel. In their reading the black horses carry famine north, and the white horses follow, meaning complete victory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/6-8.htm
- **Translation note:** The BSB says the white horses go "toward the west." The KJV and NKJV, used by Wesley, Guzik and Keil, say they go "after them," that is, following the black horses north. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/

**v. 7 (patrolling the earth)**
- Guzik notes that although two teams are focused on the north, all four also go to and fro throughout the earth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Wesley says the horses "sought to go" in the sense that they waited for orders. The one who says "Go" is Christ, who holds all power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html

**v. 8 ("given rest to My Spirit in the north")**
- Guzik: God's Spirit is at rest only when His enemies, and the enemies of His people, have been judged. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Septuagint reads "quieted my anger." Many commentators take "spirit" here to mean anger. Others see here an intimation of mercy and grace to the Jews still resident in Babylonia. https://biblehub.com/zechariah/6-8.htm
- Constable notes that Babylon had fallen to the Persians about 20 years before this, in 539 B.C. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-8.html
- Gill applies the verse to the Medes and Persians judging the Chaldeans and freeing the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-8.html
- Wesley gives two ways God's spirit is quieted: by avenging the injuries done to His people, and by bringing His people back to Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html

**vv. 9–10 (the gift from the exiles)**
- Guzik says returning exiles brought gifts from wealthy Babylon. He reports McGee's reading of the names: Heldai = "robust," Tobijah = "God's goodness," Jedaiah = "God knows." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Wesley says "the same day" means the day the men arrived. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html

**v. 11 (crowning Joshua)**
- Guzik says crowning a high priest was unthinkable, and he points to King Uzziah's leprosy in 2 Chronicles 26. He holds that Joshua, not Zerubbabel, was crowned because he was a picture of the coming King-Priest, Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the high priest's headdress is never called a crown. The crown on Joshua's head was a royal one, belonging not his own, but his whom he represented - Christ the eternal Priest, the universal King. https://biblehub.com/zechariah/6-11.htm
- Barnes notes that no crown was placed on Zerubbabel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/6-11.htm
- Bob Utley (bible.org) notes that the Hebrew word for "crown" is plural but takes a singular verb in v. 14. It may mean one double crown standing for the two offices, and it is a royal word, not the word used for a priest's headdress. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21625

**v. 12 ("the Branch")**
- Guzik calls "Branch" a familiar title for the Messiah (Isaiah 4:2, 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15). He quotes Boice: the Hebrew "Behold the man" matches Pilate's "Ecce homo." But Zechariah shows the triumphant Christ, not the humiliated one. He reads "the temple" as the temple of God's people (Ephesians 2; 1 Peter 2:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Adam Clarke rejects the view that Zerubbabel is meant. He notes that the Aramaic Targum reads "whose name is my MESSIAH," or CHRIST. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-6.html
- Gill likewise denies the verse refers to Zerubbabel and cites Jewish sources that use "Branch" as a name for the Messiah. https://studylight.org/bible/eng/gnt/zechariah/6-12.html
- Wesley: Joshua is the portrait, and Christ is the Branch himself. The material temple is far inferior to the spiritual temple Christ will build. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html

**v. 13 (a priest on his throne)**
- Guzik: priests did not sit on thrones and kings did not serve as priests, but the Branch rules as both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- Henry: Christ intercedes as priest while sitting at the Father's right hand (Hebrews 8:1). The king also has a priest's tenderness, so believers need not look at his throne with terror and amazement; for, as there is a rainbow about the throne, so he is a priest upon the throne. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/zechariah/6.htm
- Constable notes that Israel's priests never sat while ministering. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-13.html

**v. 14 (the crown as a memorial)**
- Guzik takes "Hen" (meaning "gracious") as another name for Josiah son of Zephaniah. The crown in the temple showed that Joshua was never meant to rule as king himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/
- The Bible Says: the crown would not stay on Joshua's head but would be kept in the temple as a reminder. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/zec-6-v9-15.cfm
- Wesley: the crowns were a memorial of the Messiah's certain and speedy coming. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html

**v. 15 ("those far away")**
- Henry prefers to read this as Jews and Gentiles uniting in the church, with Christ as the centre of their unity. He also mentions a view that it means Jews still in Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/zechariah/6.htm
- Wesley gives the verse a double meaning: Jews helping to build the material temple, and Gentiles coming into the spiritual temple. He stresses the condition "if you will obey." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html
- Guzik: the promise lay far in the future, but it encouraged the building work going on then. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/

---

## Part 2: Where Protestant commentators differ

**vv. 1–8: Are the chariots four empires, or angels of judgment?**
- *Four-empires view.* Henry reports a reading in which red is Babylon, black Persia, white Greece and grizzled Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-8.html Gill (Baptist) notes that Jewish writers, following the Targum, read the chariots as the four monarchies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/6-1.htm William Kelly (Brethren/dispensational) calls them an unmistakable reference to Daniel's kingdoms. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-1.html
- *Against it.* Constable mentions Kelly's view and says This seems unlikely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-1.html Keil argues that the directions given to the horses take away all support for the four-empires idea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/6-8.htm Guzik prefers to link the chariots with the horsemen of Revelation 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-6/

**v. 11: One crown or two?**
- Calvin (Reformed) insists on two crowns and calls the one-crown view false. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-9.html Wesley (Methodist) also says two: one silver, one gold. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html
- Clarke (also Methodist) cites manuscripts with the singular and concludes one crown is meant. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/zechariah-6.html

**v. 13: Who are "the two" in "peaceful counsel between the two"?**
- *The Father and the Son.* Ellicott argues the phrase can only mean two persons, the Branch and the LORD. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-13.html
- *The two offices of Christ.* Henry gives the Father-and-Son reading first but prefers this one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/zechariah/6.htm Wesley says that as priest Christ makes peace with God, and as king he delivers his people from their enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/zechariah-6.html Coffman, listing the different opinions, also favours this view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-13.html

**vv. 12–13, 15: Which temple does the Branch build, and when does he reign?**
- *The church.* Henry, Wesley and Guzik read it as the spiritual temple, the church (pages above).
- *A future millennial temple (dispensational).* Chuck Smith points to the "Kingdom Age" temple of Ezekiel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-13.html The Bible Says links it to Ezekiel 40–47 and Christ's thousand-year reign. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/zec-6-v9-15.cfm Kelly says Christ is now a priest on His Father's throne, not yet on His own. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-12.html

---

## Part 3: Other views

**Critical scholarship (Zerubbabel and the text)**
- Dummelow reports that many scholars think the crown was really meant for Zerubbabel. On this view his name was left out for political reasons, or the words "of Zerubbabel and" dropped out of v. 11. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/zechariah-6.html
- Eugene Merrill (bible.org) notes that many interpreters put Zerubbabel's name in place of Joshua's. His own translation keeps Joshua and reads v. 12 as distinguishing Joshua from "the man named Branch." https://bible.org/seriespage/zechariah-part-1-night-visions-11%E2%80%94615
- The Bridgeway commentary holds that the crown rightly belonged to Zerubbabel, the true Davidic "branch." On this view crowning the priest avoided looking like a rebellion against Persia. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-11.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) reads "There shall be a Priest upon his right hand," which implies a second figure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-13.html Keil argues against bringing a separate priest into the text. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/6-13.html

**Catholic readings**
- The Douay-Rheims reads v. 12 as BEHOLD A MAN, THE ORIENT IS HIS NAME ("Orient" means the dawn or rising). https://biblehub.com/catholic/zechariah/6-12.htm
- Haydock says the prophet showed the crown did not belong to the high priest except as a figure of the Messiah. The "man, who is also God" is called Orient because he raises up the kingdom promised to David. https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/zechariah-6.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia lists Zechariah's "Orient" or "bud" (chapters 3 and 6) among Old Testament titles for the Messiah. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14597a.htm
- Ambrose cites "My Servant, the Orient is His name" when describing Christ's service as man. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34045.htm (Cyprian quotes the parallel "Orient" text from Zechariah 3. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050712b.htm)
